This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Mississippi's U.S. Senate race has finally been called.
Democratic challenger Scott Colombe will be the state's next senator.
According to a race call by the Associated Press, Colombe is the first Democrat elected
to the Senate from the state since 1982 and the first African-American to represent Mississippi
since Reconstruction.
Elise Catrine-Greg of the Gulf States Newsroom and Mississippi Public Broadcasting reports.
Since 2016, Colombe has been a local district attorney.
His platform was on affordability, health care accessibility, saving rural hospitals,
which is a huge deal here in Mississippi.
And he said that his work as a DA in an area that leans right has really informed just
his push for bipartisanship and prioritizing issues that matter to Mississippians across
the state.
Catrine-Greg of the Gulf States Newsroom and Mississippi Public Broadcasting reporting.
North Carolina Republican Congressman Greg Murphy has conceded in his race for reelection.
As NPR's Tamara Keith reports, this is just the latest Republican seat to flip towards
Democrats in North Carolina this year.
North Carolina was one of the states that redrew its congressional district lines to
favor Republicans, but that mid-decade gerrymander has backfired spectacularly.
In the case of Murphy, his district got a little less Republican as part of an effort
to oust the Democratic congressman in the neighboring district.
Thanks to a blue tsunami, Democrats won in both districts.
Going into the midterms, Republicans held 10 House districts in North Carolina, while
Democrats held just four.
In a dramatic reversal come January, Democrats are on pace to hold 11 of the state's 14
House seats.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
A federal appeals court panel has ruled that the Justice Department cannot compel the social
media platform LinkedIn to hand over vast troves of correspondence involving journalists
simply because it's investigating a national security leak.
The opinion found that violates constitutional protections by interfering with the press,
NPR's David Falkenflick reports.
Which journalists are involved?
What secrets were disclosed?
We don't know.
We only know of the case at all because LinkedIn fought the subpoenas of information as overly
broad, likely to capture a ton of correspondence between journalists and sources that had nothing
to do with the leak.
Federal appeals court judge Harvey Wilkinson III wrote that the district court should not
have approved prosecutor searches simply because, quote, "the records requested are logistically
feasible to compile."
The ruling orders that the search be narrowed.
He also wrote that the First Amendment is first is no mere irrelevance.
He continued, "It captures both who we are as a people and what we aspire to become."
David Falkenflick, NPR News.
A rebound for A.I. stocks lifted the U.S. market today.
The S&P 500 rose more than one and a quarter percent, close to recovering all of its selloff
from last week.
The Dow added nearly half a percent.
This is NPR News.
Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases.
The crisis began in mid-May, and authorities have struggled to contain it due to armed
conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads, and violence fueled by mistrust.
What used to be the fastest passenger liner in the world is sinking, a Florida county
is now set to turn the S.S. United States into the world's largest artificial reef,
as NPR's Henry Larson reports.
The S.S. United States, launched in 1951, once transported four presidents, the Mona
Lisa and a slate of 20th century movie stars.
But after decades spent rusting, its minders settled on a deal to sink the vessel off the
coast of Okaloosa County, Florida.
Here, its massive steel hull will become hardscape for a reef on the seafloor, a marine habitat
to boost biodiversity.
To begin the process, crews opened up plugs placed in the ship's hull, filling it with
water.
The sinking is a bittersweet coda to an era of gleaming behemoths that cross the ocean
in elegant fashion.
And it's also part of an ongoing effort by coastal communities to lure thrill-seekers
away from international destinations, one that has so far generated surprising economic
benefits.
Henry Larson, NPR News.
A European spacecraft has begun inspections of an asteroid targeted by NASA four years
ago in a planetary defense test.
The European Space Agency says that the HERA spacecraft is studying didymos and its moonlit
dimorphous.
NASA's DART spacecraft slammed into dimorphous in 2022 to see whether such a move might help
save Earth one day from a killer asteroid.
This is NPR News from Washington.
